title: Capitulation
teaches: The capitulation as we trade it: a straight-down burst in a liquid stock or index, ending in a flush day whose low sits 2 ATR or more under the prior close on at least twice the usual volume, 15% or more off the 10-session high. We never buy the falling price or the flush close. We buy the undercut and reclaim of the flush low within 3 sessions, stop a few cents under the low of the day we bought, take a third at 3R and 5R, and accept the stop as the cost of being early.

walkthroughs.title: ALB, May 2010: the tiny stop
steps: ALB on 2010-05-06, the flash-crash session. The low is 17.2% under the 10-day high close and 3.94 ATR under the prior close.
Three lower closes, then a spike low. We do not buy the flush close. We wait for the turn.
On 2010-05-07 it undercuts 38.31 and closes at 39.23. The buy is the reclaim, 38.49, as a market order.
The stop is 38.26, 0.6% away. A stop that tight puts 5R only about 3% above the buy.

walkthroughs.title: OKTA, April 2025: the Monday turn
steps: On Friday 2025-04-04 OKTA's low is 23.4% under its 10-day high close, 2.67 ATR under the prior close, on 2.28x volume.
On Monday, 2025-04-07, it opens at 88.34 under the flush low, undercuts to 87.93 and closes at 91.24.
We buy the reclaim at 89.37. The stop sits a few cents under the undercut low, 87.88.
That stop is 1.7% away. Several down days into a Friday, then a Monday turn: Bracco's Monday Effect.

walkthroughs.title: BN, March 2020: the crash had one more leg
steps: BN on 2020-03-09 flushes 16.5% off its 10-day high, 3.29 ATR, on 3.03x volume.
The reclaim comes the next day. We buy 19.57 with a stop at 19.40, 0.89% away.
On 2020-03-11 the low is 18.98, through the stop. The index made a new low the same week.
The stock traded 41% under the buy. The crash had one more leg. The stop kept the loss small.

questions.q: What marks the flush day in a capitulation?
choices: A low 2+ ATR under the prior close
A close under the lower Bollinger band
A close right at the day's low
Record volume, whatever the range
questions.answer: A low 2+ ATR under the prior close
questions.why: A low 2 ATR or more under the prior close. The card also accepts a range of at least 2 ATR on the day. A climax brings wider spreads and a steeper decline, so the flush day is wide and fast. Volume is a separate test, and a band close is only supporting evidence.
questions.lesson_line: The flush day is a 2 ATR drop, not a drift.

wrong.A close under the lower Bollinger band: A band close is supporting evidence only. The flush day is measured by its low against the prior close.
wrong.A close right at the day's low: Where it closes is not the test. A climax often closes well off its low.
wrong.Record volume, whatever the range: Volume is a separate test. The day needs a low 2 ATR under the prior close, or a 2 ATR range.

questions.simple: The flush day drops hard. Its low sits 2 ATR or more under the prior close.

reasons: house: proposed card criterion, owner review is the gate
the 2 ATR threshold is a proposal that may change

questions.q: In a capitulation we buy the flush-day close.
questions.why: False. The card says do not buy the falling price or the flush close. Nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day, so buying the close is buying the knife. We wait for the turn instead.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy the falling price or the flush close.
questions.simple: False. We never buy the flush close, because nearly half of them are undercut the next day.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The daily trigger is the undercut and ___ of the flush low.
questions.why: Reclaim. Our card's daily trigger is the undercut and reclaim. Within 3 sessions after the flush day, a session trades below the flush low and then back above it. We buy at the reclaim of the flush low. The dip under the low is not the buy on its own.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut, then reclaim. The reclaim is the buy.
questions.simple: The word is reclaim, because we buy when price climbs back above the flush low after dipping under it.

reasons: the daily trigger and its 3-session window are pending D-003

questions.q: What does heavy volume at the lows say, by Kell?
choices: Fear is in; holders are giving up
The sellers are only getting started
The selling is calm and orderly
A new uptrend is starting here
questions.answer: Fear is in; holders are giving up
questions.why: Fear has set in, and traders are capitulating. Kell reads heavy volume at the lows that way. The Wyckoff tutorial says the same of a selling climax. Heavy or panicky selling by the public is absorbed by larger interests near a bottom. It is panic, not calm, and not yet a new trend.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume at the lows is panic, not control.

wrong.The selling is calm and orderly: Heavy volume at the lows is panic, not calm. A climax brings extremely heavy volume and wide spreads.
wrong.A new uptrend is starting here: Not yet. A climax must be successfully tested before it is more than a short term capitulation.
wrong.The sellers are only getting started: Kell reads it the other way: fear has set in, and traders are capitulating their positions.

questions.simple: Heavy volume at the lows means fear has set in and many holders are giving up and selling.

reasons: three publishers agree (Kell on TraderLion, Wyckoff on StockCharts, a CMT teacher on IBKR Campus)
the TraderLion archive capture and the IBKR Campus page were unreachable to WebFetch on 2026-11-12; the Wyckoff quote was re-found

questions.q: A decline on falling volume qualifies as a capitulation.
questions.why: False. The card says a decline on falling volume does not qualify. The flush day needs volume of at least 2 times the 50-day average. Such a stock can still bottom: Wyckoff notes a downtrend can end without climactic price and volume action. It just is not this setup.
questions.lesson_line: A decline on falling volume is not a capitulation.
questions.simple: False. A decline on falling volume does not qualify, because the flush day needs at least twice the usual volume.

questions.q: How much volume do we want on the flush day?
choices: At least twice the 50-day average
About 1.5 times the 50-day average
About the 50-day average volume
Any volume will do on a big drop
questions.why: At least 2 times the 50-day average. That is the floor. Ideally the flush day is the highest volume of the decline or of the year. Climaxes bring extremely heavy volume, so ordinary volume does not mark one. A decline on falling volume does not qualify at all.
questions.lesson_line: A flush needs at least twice the usual volume.

wrong.About the 50-day average volume: Ordinary volume does not mark a flush. We want at least 2 times.
wrong.Any volume will do on a big drop: Volume is one of the gates. A decline on falling volume does not qualify.
wrong.About 1.5 times the 50-day average: That falls short. The card's floor is at least 2 times the 50-day average.

questions.simple: At least twice the 50-day average, because a real panic shows up as very heavy volume.

reasons: the 2x volume is the dossier's own proposal and may change

questions.q: Tap the number for a stock, not a 3x ETF.
questions.sentence: A stock must fall at least ___ from its highest close of the last 10 sessions.
questions.why: 15%. Our card asks a stock to fall at least 15% from its highest close of the last 10 sessions. A 3x ETF needs 30% instead. Measure from the highest close, not from the intraday high.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks need 15% off the 10-session high. 3x ETFs need 30%.
questions.simple: A stock must fall at least 15% from its highest close of the last 10 sessions to count.

reasons: the 15% / 30% stretch is the dossier's proposal, waiting on the owner's review

questions.q: How far under its 50-day should an index close in a flush?
choices: At least 3 ATR
At least 2 ATR
At least 1 ATR
At least 15%
questions.why: At least 3 ATR under the 50-day SMA. That is the card's stretch for an index. Bracco finds intermediate corrections typically bottom around an average of 3 ATR below the 50-day. It is a typical zone, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: An index flush closes 3 ATR or more under its 50-day.

wrong.At least 1 ATR: The card asks for at least 3 ATR under the 50-day. One ATR falls well short.
wrong.At least 2 ATR: 2 ATR is the flush day's drop from the prior close. The index stretch is at least 3 ATR under the 50-day.
wrong.At least 15%: 15% is the stretch for a stock, from its 10-day high close. An index is measured in ATR.

questions.simple: At least 3 ATR under its 50-day, because intermediate corrections tend to bottom around there.

questions.q: A capitulation flush closes below the 5-day, the 9 EMA and the 20 EMA.
questions.why: True. Our card wants price below the 5-day SMA, the 9 EMA and the 20 EMA at the flush. If price still holds above them, that box of the card is not met. Being under them is part of the shape, not a buy signal.
questions.lesson_line: The flush leaves price under the 5-day, 9 EMA and 20 EMA.
questions.simple: True, because a real flush leaves price below the 5-day, the 9 EMA and the 20 EMA.

reasons: a proposed card criterion, waiting on the owner's review

questions.q: How many lower closes should come before the flush day?
choices: At least 2
None; a one-day shock counts
At least 10
Exactly 1
questions.why: At least 2. A capitulation is not a one-day shock out of nowhere. It comes after the stock has already been falling.
questions.lesson_line: Two or more lower closes come before the flush.

wrong.None; a one-day shock counts: A one-day shock out of nowhere is not the setup.
wrong.At least 10: The burst is a few days, not ten.
wrong.Exactly 1: One lower close is not enough. We want at least 2.

questions.q: A close below the lower Bollinger band is a buy signal.
questions.why: False. On our card, a close below the lower Bollinger band is supporting evidence only, never the trigger. Bollinger himself says a tag of the lower band is not in itself a buy signal. He adds that closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals, not reversal signals.
questions.lesson_line: A band close is evidence. The reclaim is the trigger.
questions.simple: False. A close under the lower band only shows a stretch, not a signal to buy.

questions.q: What is the taught daily trigger for a capitulation?
choices: Buy the reclaim of the flush low
Buy at the flush day's close
Buy a break of the flush high
Buy the first green day
questions.answer: Buy the reclaim of the flush low
questions.why: Undercut the flush low, then reclaim it. Within 3 sessions after the flush day, a session trades below the flush low and then back above it. We buy that reclaim. We never buy the flush close: nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day. A green day alone is not the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the reclaim of the flush low, within 3 sessions.

wrong.Buy at the flush day's close: That is the knife. Nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day.
wrong.Buy a break of the flush high: That is not our trigger. We buy the reclaim of the flush low, within 3 sessions.
wrong.Buy the first green day: A green day alone is not the trigger. A session must trade under the flush low and back above it.

questions.simple: We buy when price dips under the flush low and then climbs back above it, not at the flush close.

reasons: the daily trigger and its 3-session window are pending D-003

questions.q: A capitulation read needs a stock at $10 or more that trades $20 million a day.
questions.why: True. Our rule is to trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. The capitulation card repeats it. A cheaper or thinner stock is not a trade for us, however hard it flushed.
questions.lesson_line: Price $10 or more, $20 million a day or more.
questions.simple: True, because we only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

questions.q: Which is a level that matters under a flush?
choices: A round number, like $50
A minor low from last week
The 9 EMA on the daily chart
The lower Bollinger band
questions.why: A round number. The card lists the levels that matter. They are a prior all-time high or breakout level, a round number, or the 200-day or 50-week average. An anchored VWAP from a major low or an old gap also count. Bracco's FIGR trade washed out the $50 level and a prior high. A minor low, a short average and the lower band are not on that list.
questions.lesson_line: A flush should drop into a level that matters.

wrong.A minor low from last week: A minor low is not on the card's list of levels that matter.
wrong.The 9 EMA on the daily chart: A flush falls below the 9 EMA, so it sits above the flush. It is not a level under it.
wrong.The lower Bollinger band: A band close is supporting evidence only. The band is not on the card's list of levels.

questions.simple: A round number. The card wants a flush into a level traders watch, like $50.

questions.q: Prior close 80.00, ATR 2.50, today's low 74.60. How many ATR under the prior close is the low?
questions.why: 2.16 ATR. Take the drop, 80.00 minus 74.60, and divide it by the ATR of 2.50. That gives 2.16. Our card wants the flush day's low at least 2 ATR under the prior close, so this clears the bar.
questions.lesson_line: Drop in dollars, divided by the ATR.
questions.simple: The low is 2.16 ATR under the prior close, because the dollar drop divided by the 2.50 ATR gives 2.16.

reasons: the 2 ATR flush line is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: The highest close of the last 10 sessions was 120.00 and the flush low is 100.00. How far is the drop, in percent?
questions.why: 16.7%. Take the drop, 120.00 minus 100.00, and divide it by the high close of 120.00. That gives 16.7%. A stock needs at least 15% off its highest close of the last 10 sessions, so this one clears the stretch.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the drop from the 10-session high close.
questions.simple: The drop is 16.7% from the 120.00 high close, and that clears the 15% a stock needs.

reasons: the 15% stretch is the dossier's proposal

questions.q: QQQ's 50-day is 500 and its ATR is 8. It closes at 472. How many ATR under the 50-day is it?
questions.why: 3.5 ATR. Take the gap, 500 minus 472, and divide it by the ATR of 8. That gives 3.5. Our card wants an index to close at least 3 ATR under the 50-day SMA, so it meets the index stretch. Bracco notes that intermediate corrections typically find a tradable bottom around 3 ATR under the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Distance under the 50-day, divided by the ATR.
questions.simple: QQQ sits 3.5 ATR under its 50-day, which is past the 3 ATR an index flush needs.

reasons: the 3 ATR index stretch is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: A Wyckoff trader buys right at the selling climax.
questions.why: False. In Wyckoff's method a successful test of supply, such as a spring, is the high-probability trade, not the climax itself. A CMT teacher puts it plainly: a climax must be successfully tested before it is more than a short term capitulation.
questions.lesson_line: Even the Wyckoff school waits for the test.
questions.simple: False, because the Wyckoff trader waits for a test such as a spring and does not buy the climax itself.

reasons: two publishers agree (StockCharts Wyckoff tutorial, CMT on IBKR Campus)
the IBKR Campus page answered 403 to WebFetch on 2026-11-12; the Wyckoff quote was re-found

questions.q: Kell says trading the daily Reversal Extension at once is often best avoided.
questions.why: True. Kell says trading the daily Reversal Extension is often best avoided. We do not buy the falling price either.
questions.lesson_line: The early buy is the risky buy.

questions.q: Bracco notes that notable capitulations and turns have occurred on a Monday.
questions.why: True. Bracco writes that through his studies notable capitulations and turns have occurred on a Monday. It is his observation, not a rule. Our card notes the shape: several straight down days into a Friday, then a gap down on Monday.
questions.lesson_line: Bracco has seen notable turns on Mondays, after several down days.
questions.simple: True, because Bracco writes that in his studies notable capitulations and turns have come on a Monday.

reasons: Bracco's Monday list has a typo the dossier flags (D-015); no date is keyed

questions.q: A capitulation needs an RS rating of 80 or more.
questions.why: False. Our leader rule asks for an RS rating of 80 or more, but mean-reversion and parabolic trades are exempt. The capitulation card says there is no RS requirement. Bracco still uses this kind of long to get exposure to powerful, trending leaders.
questions.lesson_line: No RS requirement here, though leaders are preferred.
questions.simple: False, because mean-reversion trades like this one are exempt from our RS 80 leader rule.

questions.q: Buy the close, or wait?
choices: Wait for the undercut and reclaim
Buy the close; record volume
Wait a week for it to settle
Buy tomorrow's open regardless
questions.story: The flush day closes at its low on record volume, 4 ATR under yesterday's close. It looks like the bottom.
questions.answer: Wait for the undercut and reclaim
questions.why: Wait for the undercut and reclaim. We do not buy the falling price or the flush close, even on record volume. Nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day. The trigger comes after: within 3 sessions, a session trades below the flush low and back above it. We buy that reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the turn, not the knife.

wrong.Buy the close; record volume: Record volume shows the panic. It does not show the low is in.
wrong.Wait a week for it to settle: The trigger has a window: within 3 sessions of the flush. A week can miss it.
wrong.Buy tomorrow's open regardless: A blind open is not a trigger. The reclaim of the flush low is.

questions.simple: Wait. The flush close is often not the low, so we buy only when price breaks the low and climbs back.

deeper.trap: Record volume tempts you to buy the close. It shows the panic, not the low. The card warns that nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day. Buying the knife, not the turn, is how it loses. Wait for a session to trade under the flush low and back above it.

reasons: keys the daily trigger, pending D-003

questions.q: Where do you buy?
choices: On the reclaim back over 64.20
At 63.95, the new low of the day
At the close of the flush day
On a break of the flush high
questions.story: The flush low is 64.20. The next day price trades down to 63.95, then climbs back above 64.20.
questions.why: On the reclaim back above 64.20, the flush low. The dip to 63.95 is the undercut. The buy comes when price trades back above the flush low. The stop then goes a few cents under 63.95, the low of the session you bought in. Buying the flush close is the knife: nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut the flush low, then buy the reclaim.

wrong.At the close of the flush day: That is the knife. Nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day.
wrong.On a break of the flush high: That is not our trigger. We buy the reclaim of the flush low.
wrong.At 63.95, the new low of the day: That is buying the falling price. We wait for the reclaim of the flush low.

questions.simple: Buy when price climbs back over 64.20, the flush low, because that reclaim is the trigger.

reasons: the daily trigger is pending D-003 and the setup's stop D-008; keyed on the settled house stop

questions.q: Reclaim at 38.49, undercut low 38.31, stop at 38.26. How far is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 0.6%. Take the stop distance, 38.49 minus 38.26, and divide it by the entry of 38.49. That gives 0.6%. The stop sits a few cents under the undercut low of 38.31. That is very tight, well inside the usual stop of about 3% of the buy.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sits a few cents under the undercut low.
questions.simple: The stop is only 0.6% away, because it sits a few cents under the undercut low.

deeper.example: A tiny stop changes what the targets mean. ALB's stop was 0.6% under the buy, so 5R was only about 3% above it. The bounce did not need to be big to pay. It also means a small dip can reach the stop, so the plan has to accept that.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and an example the owner has not reviewed (D-007); stop width is D-041

questions.q: Entry 38.49, stop 38.26. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 39.64. One R is the risk per share, 38.49 minus 38.26. Add five of those to the entry of 38.49 and you reach 39.64. 5R is a mark to measure by. Selling at about 5 to 10R is often best.
questions.lesson_line: 5R is five risk units above the entry.
questions.simple: 5R is 39.64, because five times the risk per share, added to the 38.49 entry, lands there.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51) and the ALB example (D-007)

questions.q: Is this a panic flush?
choices: No; it is an earnings reaction
Yes; earnings fear is panic
Yes; 20% is deep enough
No; it fell too slowly
questions.story: A leader drops 20% in two days right after it reports earnings.
questions.answer: No; it is an earnings reaction
questions.why: No. It is an earnings reaction. The card says an earnings reaction is not a panic flush, so we keep the two apart. The size and speed of the drop do not decide it. The report does. In our scan, 150 of 346 above-200-day hits with report dates had a report inside the flush window.
questions.lesson_line: Keep earnings reactions apart from panic flushes.

wrong.No; it fell too slowly: Speed is not the test here. The report inside the flush window sets it apart.
wrong.Yes; earnings fear is panic: The card keeps them apart. An earnings reaction is not a panic flush.
wrong.Yes; 20% is deep enough: 20% clears the 15% stretch, but that is one test. The report inside the window rules it out.

questions.simple: No. A drop right after earnings is a reaction to news, and we keep that apart from a panic flush.

reasons: scan numbers that change with a rescan

questions.q: Buy the reclaim?
choices: No; the report is 2 sessions away
Yes; the reclaim is the trigger
Yes, but at half size to be safe
No; earnings mean skip it for a month
questions.story: The reclaim triggers two sessions before the company reports earnings.
questions.answer: No; the report is 2 sessions away
questions.why: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and our card says the same for this setup. Two sessions away is inside that window. A clean trigger does not override it, and a smaller size does not either.
questions.lesson_line: A clean trigger still waits out the report.

wrong.Yes; the reclaim is the trigger: The trigger does not override the report window.
wrong.Yes, but at half size to be safe: The rule is no new buy in the 3 sessions before a report. Size does not change that.
wrong.No; earnings mean skip it for a month: The window is the 3 sessions before a report, not a month.

questions.simple: No, because we never start a new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.

questions.q: Buy now?
choices: No; 4.8% above, past the 4% limit
Yes; the setup is still intact
Yes, with a wider stop to fit it
No; never buy above the trigger price
questions.story: The trigger price is 50.00. You look late and the stock trades at 52.40.
questions.why: No. 52.40 is 4.8% above the 50.00 trigger. Our rule: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the trigger, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Past 4%, the trade is a pass.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the trigger, it is a pass.

wrong.Yes; the setup is still intact: An intact setup still has a chase limit. No buy more than 4% above the trigger.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop to fit it: Chasing already stretches the distance to the stop and shrinks the size. The rule is no buy past 4%.
wrong.No; never buy above the trigger price: The limit is 4% above the trigger, not zero. A buy up to 4% above it is allowed.

questions.simple: No, because 52.40 is 4.8% above the 50.00 trigger, past our 4% chase limit.

deeper.counter: Half size or a wider stop feels like a fix for a late look. It is not. The stop stays under the trigger, so a higher buy only adds distance and cuts the shares. The rule is a line: past 4% above the trigger, the trade is a pass, and you wait for a new trigger.

questions.q: Is that a trigger?
choices: No; it is evidence, not a trigger
Yes; a close outside is the trigger
Yes, after three closes outside
No; bands never matter at all
questions.story: The stock closes under the lower Bollinger band for the second day in a row. A friend calls it a buy signal.
questions.answer: No; it is evidence, not a trigger
questions.why: No. A close under the lower band is evidence of a stretch, never the trigger. Bollinger says a tag of the lower band is not in itself a buy signal. Closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals, not reversal signals. More closes outside can mean the trend is still running.
questions.lesson_line: A stretched close is not a turn.

wrong.Yes; a close outside is the trigger: A band tag is not in itself a buy signal.
wrong.Yes, after three closes outside: More closes outside the band can mean the trend is walking down it.
wrong.No; bands never matter at all: They help as evidence of a stretch. They are just not the trigger.

questions.simple: No. Closing under the lower band shows a stretch, but it is not the signal to buy.

deeper.trap: A second close under the band feels like more proof of a bottom. Bollinger reads it the other way: closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals. On our card the band is supporting evidence only. Wait for the turn.

questions.q: What does that tell you?
choices: An early warning; the stop rules
A buy signal; add on the dip
Nothing; one candle is minor
Move the stop down a bit
questions.story: You bought the reclaim. The first bounce day closes in the lower third of its range.
questions.answer: An early warning; the stop rules
questions.why: An early warning. Our card names it: the bounce stalls on the first day and closes in its lower third. It does not move the stop or change the size. The stop is the exit, it only moves up, and we never average down.
questions.lesson_line: A weak first bounce is a warning. Keep the stop.

wrong.A buy signal; add on the dip: We never average down. It is full size at one price.
wrong.Nothing; one candle is minor: Our card names this stall the early warning. It is not nothing.
wrong.Move the stop down a bit: The stop only moves up, never down.

questions.simple: It is an early warning that the bounce is weak, but the stop still decides the exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and a proposed card criterion

questions.q: Is this a capitulation?
choices: No; there was no burst before it
Yes; it passes all of the numbers
Yes; three weeks down is the burst
No; it needs 20% off the high
questions.story: A stock chops lower for three weeks, with up and down days mixed, no gaps and no big days. Then it drops 2.61 ATR on 2.02x volume, 15.3% off its 10-day high.
questions.answer: No; there was no burst before it
questions.why: No. The last day passes the numbers: 2.61 ATR, 2.02x volume and 15.3% off the 10-day high. But a slow grind or a controlled mark down is not a capitulation. Look left: three weeks of choppy selling is not a burst. Bracco saw no fear or panic in a choppy, controlled mark down.
questions.lesson_line: Look left. A slow grind is not a burst.

wrong.Yes; it passes all of the numbers: The day's numbers pass. A slow grind before it is not a capitulation.
wrong.Yes; three weeks down is the burst: A slow grind or a controlled mark down is not a burst.
wrong.No; it needs 20% off the high: The card asks for 15% off the 10-day high. 15.3% clears it.

questions.simple: No. The stock slid slowly for weeks, and a slow grind is not the fast burst a capitulation needs.

deeper.example: MS is the dossier's case. Its drop was 2.61 ATR on 2.02x volume, 15.3% off the 10-day high, into the 200-day. Every number passed. But it came at the end of a controlled three-week mark down, not a burst. The card's line: no burst, no capitulation.

reasons: the burst idea is held under D-002

questions.q: Capitulation, or not?
choices: No; no lower closes came first
Yes; a 20% one-day drop is a flush
Yes; heavy volume is enough alone
No; a 20% fall is too shallow
questions.story: A stock closes flat or higher every day for a week. Then it falls 20% in a single session on heavy volume.
questions.answer: No; no lower closes came first
questions.why: No. The card wants at least 2 lower closes before the flush day. This stock closed flat or higher all week. Then it fell 20% in one session: a one-day shock out of nowhere. The size of the drop and the volume do not fix that.
questions.lesson_line: A one-day shock with no lower closes first is not this setup.

wrong.Yes; a 20% one-day drop is a flush: The size is not enough. It needs a run of lower closes first.
wrong.Yes; heavy volume is enough alone: Volume is one gate, not the only one.
wrong.No; a 20% fall is too shallow: Depth is not the problem. The card asks for a fall of at least 15%, and 20% clears it.

questions.simple: No. A one-day drop out of a calm week is a shock, and the card wants at least 2 lower closes first.

questions.q: Does the volume qualify?
choices: No; the flush needs 2 times the average
Yes; volume is up
Yes; three down days is enough
No; it must be 10 times
questions.story: A leader is down three days in a row. The flush day trades only 1.3 times its 50-day average volume.
questions.answer: No; the flush needs 2 times the average
questions.why: No. Flush-day volume needs to be at least 2 times the 50-day average, and ideally the highest of the decline.
questions.lesson_line: Modest volume is a pullback, not a panic.

wrong.Yes; volume is up: Up a little is not a panic. The bar is 2 times.
wrong.Yes; three down days is enough: Down days are one gate. Volume is another.

questions.q: Does it pass?
choices: No; volume is just under the 2x bar
Yes; 1.96 rounds up to the 2x bar
Yes; volume is optional on a big ATR
No; the ATR is too small to count
questions.story: A flush day: 2.13 ATR, 15.2% off the 10-day high, above the 200-day. Volume is 1.96 times the 50-day average.
questions.answer: No; volume is just under the 2x bar
questions.why: No. Our card asks flush-day volume of at least 2 times the 50-day average, and 1.96 is under it. The rest of the shape is there: 2.13 ATR and 15.2% off the high. A near miss is still a miss. The 2 times line is the card's proposal, and the test is the number as written.
questions.lesson_line: A near miss is still a miss.

wrong.Yes; 1.96 rounds up to the 2x bar: The test is the number, not a rounding. 1.96 is under 2.
wrong.Yes; volume is optional on a big ATR: Volume is a gate. A big ATR does not stand in for it.

questions.simple: It fails, because 1.96 times the average volume is under the 2 times bar, and a rule is a line.

deeper.trap: The trap is rounding. 1.96 looks like 2, and every other part of the shape is there: 2.13 ATR and 15.2% off the high. But the volume bar is a line, and 1.96 sits under it. Round one gate today and you will round the next one tomorrow.

reasons: the 2x volume bar is the dossier's proposal, and the LLY near miss is from the owner-unreviewed dossier (D-007)

questions.q: Which rule stops the buy?
choices: The 200-day rule: where price sits
The stretch rule: the fall off the high
The flush rule: the drop in ATR
The volume rule: versus the average
questions.story: The reclaim closes 15.9% under the 200-day. The stock slid for two months, then dropped 2.19 ATR on 3.48x volume, 17.6% off its high.
questions.why: The 200-day rule. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. Only an index or a levered ETF may go under it, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. The flush, the volume and the stretch all clear their bars: 2.19 ATR, 3.48 times and 17.6%.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no stock long.

wrong.The stretch rule: the fall off the high: 17.6% off the high clears the 15% stretch.

questions.simple: The 200-day rule stops it, because below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26); what counts as a parabolic long is held (D-002, D-009, D-119)

questions.q: Bulkowski found that nearly half of one-day collapses make a lower low the next day.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski found that forty-six percent of his one-day collapse events make a lower low the next day. Then 17% continue lower the day after, then 9%, then 3%. So buying the first close is often early. That is why we wait for the turn instead of buying the knife.
questions.lesson_line: Nearly half make a lower low the next day.
questions.simple: True. In his study, nearly half made a lower low the next day, so buying the first close is often early.

reasons: rests on Bulkowski, whose site asks not to be used for AI training (source policy open)

questions.q: After a big one-day drop, Bulkowski's average bounce is how big, and how long?
choices: 28% over 23 days
5% over 2 days
60% over 6 months
No bounce at all
questions.why: 28% over 23 days. That is Bulkowski's average bounce, from the event low to the bounce high, after a one-day collapse. It does not last: price then resumes declining, averaging 30% from the bounce high in 49 days. So the bounce is a trade, not a new trend. Bracco also treats his mean reversion bounces as short lived trades.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce is a trade, not a new trend.

wrong.5% over 2 days: That is far smaller and faster than his average. It is 28% over 23 days.
wrong.60% over 6 months: Too big and too long. The bounce averages 28% in 23 days, then price falls again.
wrong.No bounce at all: There is a bounce. Then price resumes declining, about 30% in 49 days.

questions.simple: His average bounce is 28% over 23 days, and then price tends to fall again.

reasons: rests on Bulkowski, whose site asks not to be used for AI training (source policy open)

questions.q: In Bulkowski's own trades, what share of buys in stage 4, the downtrend, made money?
questions.why: 24.41%. In Bulkowski's own trades, just 24.41% of the stocks bought in stage 4, the downtrend, made money. In stage 1, 69.3% did. It is one trader's record, not a market-wide study. It fits our rule against longs under the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Buying a downtrend loses most of the time.

wrong.69.3%: That is the share of stage 1 buys that made money.
wrong.75.59%: That is about the share of stage 4 buys that did not make money.

questions.simple: Only 24.41% of his stage 4 buys made money, far fewer than the 69.3% in stage 1.

reasons: rests on one publisher (Bulkowski); the quote was re-found on 2026-11-12; his site carries a notice against AI training (owner flag)

questions.q: Buy the huge volume now?
choices: Wait; the low broke the next day
Buy now; the volume is huge
Buy half now
Buy the next open
questions.story: A stock falls 77% in 3 days on 7.0x volume. Bracco says a long may set up in the next 1-2 weeks.
questions.answer: Wait; the low broke the next day
questions.why: Wait. Bracco said 1-2 weeks, and the low broke the next day. The stock traded 25% under it within 5 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Even a 77% fall can fall further. Wait for the turn.

wrong.Buy now; the volume is huge: Huge volume showed the panic. It did not show the low.
wrong.Buy half now: Half a knife is still a knife.
wrong.Buy the next open: The next day broke the low.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Out; 19.30 is 3.5R down, past 2R
Set the stop at 19.30, the 30-min low
Hold; it should bounce back soon
Add at 19.30 to average down
questions.story: You bought at 20.00 with a stop at 19.80. It gaps down and opens at 19.70, under the stop. The first 30-minute low is 19.30.
questions.why: Out. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. There is a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. One R here is 20.00 minus 19.80. The 30-minute low of 19.30 sits 3.5R under the entry, past the ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop caps at 2R. Past that, leave.

wrong.Hold; it should bounce back soon: Past 2R in the first 30 minutes, the rule is to get out, not to wait.
wrong.Add at 19.30 to average down: We never average down. It is the full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.Set the stop at 19.30, the 30-min low: That is the gap rule without its ceiling. Past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you get out.

questions.simple: Get out, because the first 30 minutes took the loss to 3.5R, past the 2R ceiling.

deeper.trap: The gap rule lets the stop move to the first 30-minute low. It does not let the loss grow without limit. Here that low is 3.5R under the entry, past the 2R ceiling, so you are out. Hoping for a bounce is the move the ceiling exists to stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 and its 2R ceiling)

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Sell part into the gap at the open
Wait for a pullback to the 20 EMA
Hold everything and let it run
Add more at 26.00 on the gap
questions.story: You bought at 22.13 with a stop at 21.72. 5R is 24.18. The next day opens at 26.00.
questions.answer: Sell part into the gap at the open
questions.why: Sell part into the gap at the open. The open of 26.00 is far past the 5R line of 24.18, in the 5 to 10R zone where selling is often best. How much to sell is a judgment. MP opened there, then closed at 21.94, through its stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap far past 5R is a chance to sell into strength.

wrong.Wait for a pullback to the 20 EMA: A pullback may never come. A big gap is a chance to sell.
wrong.Hold everything and let it run: Holding it all gave back the gain. MP closed through its stop.
wrong.Add more at 26.00 on the gap: We never add. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Sell part into the gap at the open, because the open is far past 5R and a gap is a good time to sell.

deeper.trap: The open looked like a big win: 26.00 against a 5R line of 24.18. MP then closed at 21.94, through its stop. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open, before the day can take it back. Waiting to see if it runs is how the gain is lost.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63) and the MP example from the owner-unreviewed dossier (D-007)

questions.q: What sets the first sell of a winner?
choices: A judgment, often a 3 to 7 day push
A fixed third of the shares at 3R
A judgment, best made on the buy day
A fixed half of the shares at 5R
questions.answer: A judgment, often a 3 to 7 day push
questions.why: A judgment. The first sell depends on a variety of factors, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3 to 7 day push.

wrong.A fixed third of the shares at 3R: That was an older rule. It is not fixed. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.A judgment, best made on the buy day: Day 1 is the day we very rarely sell. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.A fixed half of the shares at 5R: Nothing is fixed. The first sell is part of the position, chosen by judgment.

questions.simple: A judgment call, often a sale into a push on day 3 or later, not a fixed third at 3R.

reasons: trim at the averages held under D-013

questions.q: We move the stop to breakeven at 2R because these bounces fade.
questions.why: True. For a capitulation the card moves the stop to breakeven at 2R. Our house rule allows anywhere from 2R to 5R. The card picks the low end because these bounces fade.
questions.lesson_line: These bounces fade, so breakeven comes early.
questions.simple: True. These bounces tend to fade, so the stop moves up to breakeven early, at 2R.

reasons: house: proposed card rule inside the B19 window

questions.q: If a capitulation buy dips toward the stop, add to average down.
questions.why: False. Never average down. Our rule is the full size at one price with one stop. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. Bracco writes that he never adds when he is down.
questions.lesson_line: Never average down. One price, one stop.
questions.simple: False. We never average down, because we buy the full size once, at one price, with one stop.

questions.q: How do we trail the last third?
choices: Higher lows, then the 10-day
A trailing stop on the 200-day
A fixed 10% stop under the buy
Sell it all at 5R instead
questions.why: Under each higher daily low, until price closes back above the 10-day. After that, sell on a close below the 10-day. Our default trail is the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. The card adapts it for this bounce.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the lows, then the 10-day.

wrong.A trailing stop on the 200-day: The card trails the higher daily lows, then the 10-day, not the 200-day.
wrong.A fixed 10% stop under the buy: A fixed stop does not follow the bounce. The card trails the higher daily lows.
wrong.Sell it all at 5R instead: At 5R we sell the second third. The last third is trailed.

questions.simple: Under each higher daily low at first, then we sell on a close under the 10-day average.

reasons: house: proposed card rule (cap.trail) on the E52 default

questions.q: Bracco treats these as short lived trades, not held longer than 1-3 days.
questions.why: True. Bracco writes that these are short lived trades, not meant to be held longer than 1-3 days. He wrote it about his rubber band longs, a mean reversion play. It is his note, not one of our rules.
questions.lesson_line: Treat the bounce as a short trade, not a new trend.
questions.simple: True. Bracco writes that these bounce trades are short lived, not meant to last more than 1-3 days.

reasons: the time stop is held under D-019
sits beside the house trail of the last third

questions.q: Which backdrop does our card want for a market-wide flush?
choices: VIX up fast to 30, breadth washed out
VIX up fast to 30, breadth near highs
VIX falling from 30, breadth washed out
VIX calm on a slow drift lower
questions.answer: VIX up fast to 30, breadth washed out
questions.why: The VIX up fast toward 30 with washed-out breadth. The card wants fear high and rising fast, a VIX spike toward 30 or more. It wants T2108 near or under 15% to 20%. Bracco says a fast move up into 30 is a time to watch for a mean reversion trade. A falling VIX or strong breadth is not that backdrop.
questions.lesson_line: A real flush has fear and washed-out breadth behind it.

wrong.VIX up fast to 30, breadth near highs: The fear is there, but breadth is not washed out. The card wants T2108 near or under 15% to 20%.
wrong.VIX falling from 30, breadth washed out: The card wants fear high and rising fast, a VIX spike toward 30 or more.
wrong.VIX calm on a slow drift lower: A slow, controlled mark down with calm fear is not a capitulation.

questions.simple: Fear rising fast toward a VIX of 30, with breadth washed out, is the backdrop the card wants.

questions.q: What does Bracco say markets typically do to big support areas?
choices: Undercut them first
Hold them to the tick
Bounce just above them
Stall at them for weeks
questions.why: Undercut them first. Bracco writes that markets typically like to undercut big support areas before reclaiming them, if they do. Our card's daily trigger looks for the same thing: a session trades below the flush low and then back above it. The reclaim is not certain.
questions.lesson_line: Big support is usually undercut before it is reclaimed.

wrong.Hold them to the tick: He says big support is typically undercut, not held exactly.
wrong.Bounce just above them: He says markets typically go under big support first.
wrong.Stall at them for weeks: He describes an undercut, then a reclaim if it comes, not a long stall.

questions.simple: Undercut them first. Big support usually breaks first, and price may then climb back over it.

reasons: keys the daily trigger, pending D-003

questions.q: Which setup's trigger is this?
choices: Capitulation; within 3 sessions
Parabolic Long; the VWAP reclaim
Mean Reversion; a dip to the 50-day
Oops Reversal; the gap under the low
questions.story: A stock flushes 2.4 ATR on 2.6x volume, 18% off its 10-day high. Two sessions later it undercuts the flush low and closes back above it. You buy the reclaim.
questions.why: Capitulation. A capitulation needs a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume and 15% or more off the 10-session high. This one has all three. It is bought on the undercut and reclaim of the flush low within 3 sessions. Here the reclaim came two sessions later. A parabolic long is bought that day, on the VWAP reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions. The reclaim after the flush is Capitulation.

wrong.Parabolic Long; the VWAP reclaim: A parabolic long is bought the same day, on the VWAP reclaim. This reclaim came two sessions later.
wrong.Mean Reversion; a dip to the 50-day: The flush is 18% off the 10-day high on 2.6x volume, a capitulation's shape. Nothing here touches the 50-day.
wrong.Oops Reversal; the gap under the low: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low in an orderly pullback. This story has no gap.

questions.simple: It is Capitulation, because it was bought on an undercut and reclaim days after the flush, not the same day.

deeper.trap: Both triggers are a reclaim, so the word alone does not tell them apart. Count the sessions. A parabolic long is bought the same day on the VWAP reclaim. A capitulation waits for a session that trades under the flush low and back above it, within 3 sessions. Here that came two sessions later.

reasons: the two triggers are pending D-003 and the setup map D-002 (Capitulation and the Parabolic Long may be one unit)

questions.q: Capitulation, or something milder?
choices: Milder; the stretch is too small
Capitulation; heavy volume is enough
Capitulation; it hit its 50-day
Parabolic Long; it fell 6% in a day
questions.story: A leader drops 6% in one day into its 50-day on heavy volume. It is 7% off its 10-day high.
questions.answer: Milder; the stretch is too small
questions.why: Milder. A capitulation needs a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume and 15% or more off the 10-session high. This stock is only 7% off its 10-day high. A one-day drop into a level in a leader is often a mean-reversion leader flush, a different setup.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stretch. 7% is a pullback.

wrong.Capitulation; heavy volume is enough: Volume is one gate. The stretch is another, and 7% is short of 15%.
wrong.Capitulation; it hit its 50-day: Hitting the 50-day does not make it one. The stretch is far short of 15%.
wrong.Parabolic Long; it fell 6% in a day: Our parabolic long is a burst down. A one-day drop into a level in a leader is often a mean-reversion flush.

questions.simple: It is milder, because 7% off the high is far short of the 15% a capitulation needs.

deeper.counter: Heavy volume into the 50-day feels like panic, but measure first. 7% off the 10-day high is far short of 15%. A one-day drop into a level in a leader is often a mean-reversion leader flush, a different setup with its own rules.

reasons: the 15% stretch and 2x volume are the dossier's proposals

questions.q: Capitulation, or something else?
choices: An undercut and rally, not a flush
A capitulation; it broke a level
A parabolic long off a fast fall
An Oops Reversal; closed back up
questions.story: A stock in an ordinary pullback opens flat, then dips 1% under a visible level. Its 50-day is not falling and volume is light. It closes back above the level.
questions.answer: An undercut and rally, not a flush
questions.why: An undercut and rally, not a capitulation. A U&R undercuts a visible level after an ordinary dip, in a stock whose 50-day is not falling. It needs no volume. A capitulation reclaims its own flush low after a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume. A 1% dip on light volume is not a flush.
questions.lesson_line: A small dip and a reclaim is a U&R. A flush is bigger.

wrong.A capitulation; it broke a level: A capitulation needs a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume, not a 1% dip.
wrong.A parabolic long off a fast fall: There was no fast fall. It was an ordinary pullback on light volume.
wrong.An Oops Reversal; closed back up: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low. This stock opened flat, with no gap.

questions.simple: An undercut and rally. It was a small dip on light volume, not a big flush on heavy volume.

deeper.trap: Both setups undercut a level and close back above it, so the reclaim alone cannot tell them apart. Check what came before. A capitulation needs a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume. A U&R comes after an ordinary dip in a stock whose 50-day is not falling, and needs no volume.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: An Oops Reversal
A capitulation flush
A Wyckoff spring
A parabolic long
questions.story: A stock gaps under yesterday's low in an orderly pullback and reclaims it the same day on a narrow range.
questions.why: An Oops Reversal. An Oops gaps under the prior day's low in an orderly pullback. A capitulation flush is 2 ATR or more on 2x volume at the end of a 15% fall. A narrow range in an orderly pullback has none of that. A spring takes price below the low of a trading range, and there is no range here.
questions.lesson_line: Orderly pullback and a narrow range is an Oops, not a flush.

wrong.A Wyckoff spring: A spring takes price below the low of a trading range. This stock was in an orderly pullback.
wrong.A parabolic long: There is no burst down before it.
wrong.A capitulation flush: A capitulation flush is 2 ATR or more on 2x volume at the end of a 15% fall. This was a narrow range.

questions.simple: An Oops Reversal. It is a small gap and reclaim in a calm pullback, not a big flush at the end of a fall.

deeper.trap: The trap is the gap. A capitulation and an Oops can both open under a low and close back above it. Measure the day: a capitulation flush is 2 ATR or more on 2x volume at the end of a 15% fall. A gap and reclaim on a narrow range in an orderly pullback is an Oops.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A Wyckoff spring; there is a range
A capitulation; it dipped under a level
A parabolic long; it broke the floor
An Oops Reversal; it closed back inside
questions.story: A stock sits in a flat 30-session range. One day it dips 0.5 ATR under the floor, with no gap, and closes back inside.
questions.answer: A Wyckoff spring; there is a range
questions.why: A Wyckoff spring. A flat range sits behind the dip, and the stock closed back inside it. A capitulation has no range behind it: it is a straight fall, and the 2 ATR flush is the setup. Nothing here gaps, so it is not an Oops.
questions.lesson_line: A range behind the dip is a spring. A straight fall is a capitulation.

wrong.A capitulation; it dipped under a level: A capitulation is a straight fall with no range behind it.
wrong.A parabolic long; it broke the floor: Our parabolic long is a burst down. This stock sat flat in a range and dipped once.
wrong.An Oops Reversal; it closed back inside: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low in an orderly pullback. This did not gap, and a flat range is no pullback.

questions.simple: It is a Wyckoff spring, because a flat range sits behind the dip, while a capitulation is a straight fall.

deeper.trap: Both shapes dip under a level and close back above it, so the dip alone does not tell them apart. Look at what came before. A spring has a flat range behind it. A capitulation has no range: it is a straight fall that ends in a 2 ATR flush.

reasons: lookalike tells are proposed card rows, pending on their own cards

questions.q: Capitulation, or something else?
choices: A moving-average pullback
A capitulation low
A parabolic long
An Oops off the EMA
questions.story: A leader drifts six sessions on light volume, with no gaps, to its rising 20 EMA and bounces.
questions.why: A moving-average pullback. On our card that lookalike is a 2 to 8 session pullback to a rising 20 or 50-day on light volume. A capitulation falls through the 5, 9 and 20-day on 2x volume with a 2 ATR flush bar. This leader drifted six sessions on light volume and held its rising 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet drift to a rising average is a pullback.

wrong.A capitulation low: A capitulation falls through the short averages on heavy volume. This one held the 20 EMA.
wrong.A parabolic long: A parabolic long needs a burst down. This was a quiet drift.
wrong.An Oops off the EMA: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low. This stock drifted with no gaps.

questions.simple: A pullback. A quiet drift on light volume to a rising average is not a panic flush.

deeper.counter: Keep the same rising 20 EMA but change the fall. Say the stock had dropped through the 5, 9 and 20-day on 2x volume with a 2 ATR flush bar. Then it would read as a capitulation. Quiet volume and a held average make it a pullback.

questions.q: Is this a capitulation long?
choices: No; the selling is informed
Yes; the volume is huge
Yes; 40% is a deep flush
No; it fell too far too fast
questions.story: A stock falls 40% in three days after the company admits accounting fraud. Volume is huge.
questions.why: No. A real business break, such as fraud or a guidance collapse, is not this setup. The selling is informed: sellers are reacting to news about the business. A selling climax is heavy or panicky selling by the public. Huge volume and a 40% fall do not change that.
questions.lesson_line: Informed selling is not a capitulation.

wrong.Yes; the volume is huge: Huge volume shows selling, not whether it is forced or informed.
wrong.Yes; 40% is a deep flush: Depth is not the test. The reason for the selling is.
wrong.No; it fell too far too fast: Depth is not a veto. The card asks for a fall of at least 15%. The reason for the selling rules this out.

questions.simple: No. The stock fell because of real bad news, so the sellers know something, and that is not a panic.

deeper.trap: Fraud news brings the same numbers a flush shows: huge volume and a deep, fast fall. That is why the numbers alone cannot clear it. Ask why it fell. When the business itself broke, the card calls the selling informed, not panic, and it is not this setup.

questions.q: What does the index tell you?
choices: Another leg down may come
The bounce is likely confirmed
The stop can safely come off
It may be time to add shares
questions.story: You hold a leader's reclaim after a 16.5% flush. The same week the index makes a new low on rising volume.
questions.why: Another leg down may come. The card lists a new index low on rising volume, while you hold, as an invalidation. BN is the dossier's case: bought on the reclaim, it was stopped on day 1. The index made a new low the same week, and the stock traded 41% under the buy. Keep the stop. Never add.
questions.lesson_line: A new index low while you hold is a warning.

wrong.The bounce is likely confirmed: A new index low says the opposite. The selling may not be done.
wrong.The stop can safely come off: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.It may be time to add shares: Never average down. It is the full size at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Another leg down may come. A new low in the index while you hold warns that the selling is not done.

questions.q: What is the warning sign?

The volume was too high
The stop was too wide
The flush was too deep

questions.q: With a typical stop of 1.7%, about how big a bounce is 3R?
choices: About 5%
About 1.7%
About 9%
About 17%
questions.why: About 5%. One R is the stop distance, so 3R is three times it. Three times 1.7% is about 5%. Our scan's median stop is 1.7%, so 3R is about a 5% bounce and 5R about 9%. A tight stop puts the R targets close.
questions.lesson_line: Tight stops mean short targets. 3R is about a 5% bounce.

wrong.About 1.7%: That is one R, not three.
wrong.About 17%: That is far past 3R. Three times 1.7% is about 5%.

questions.simple: About 5%. Three times a 1.7% stop is about 5%, so the first target is close.

deeper.trap: A tight stop makes a big R count feel like a big move. It is not. With the scan's median stop of 1.7%, 3R is about a 5% bounce and 5R about 9%. ALB shows the extreme: with its tiny stop, 5R was only 3% above the buy.

questions.q: In our scan of 2,220 reclaims, about what share reached 3R before the stop?

About a quarter
About nine in ten
Almost none
questions.why: About half: 52.3% reached 3R and 43.1% reached 5R before the stop. That is a fixed stop with no trims.

wrong.About nine in ten: 52.3% reached 3R, and 81% were stopped at some point.

questions.q: 81% were stopped at some point, yet 52.3% reached 3R. Why?
choices: Fixed stop, so fades come back
The scan's stop was far too wide
3R is just a bad target here
3R was counted after the stop hit
questions.answer: Fixed stop, so fades come back
questions.why: Because the scan's stop never moves. Of 2,220 reclaims, 52.3% reached 3R before the stop, yet 81% were stopped at some point in 60 sessions. questions.lesson_line: Bounces fade. Sell into strength, then protect the rest.

wrong.The scan's stop was far too wide: The median stop was tight, about 1.7%.
wrong.3R is just a bad target here: 52.3% reached it. The point is what happens after.
wrong.3R was counted after the stop hit: The scan counts 3R only when it came before the stop.

questions.simple: Many bounces hit 3R and then faded back to a stop that never moved, so both numbers are true.

deeper.example: Picture a bounce that reaches 3R, then fades. In the scan the stop never moved, so the fade came back and hit it. That one trade counts in both numbers: it reached 3R and it was stopped. With our plan, part is sold into strength and the stop moves up to breakeven. The same path then keeps a gain. questions.why: Market 38.49; stop 38.26. Entries are market orders, so you buy as price reclaims, at 38.49. The stop goes a few cents under the undercut low of 38.31, the low of the session you bought in. The first sell is a judgment and is not part of this order.
questions.lesson_line: Write the entry and stop before the buy.

wrong.Limit 39.23; stop 38.31: We buy as price trades through the trigger, never at the close, and a stop on the low is too tight.
wrong.Market 38.31; stop 37.00: 38.31 is the undercut price, not the reclaim, and a stop at 37.00 is far too wide.
wrong.Market 38.49; stop 38.31: A stop exactly on the low is not a few cents under it.

questions.simple: Buy at market on the reclaim and put the stop a few cents under the undercut low.

deeper.trap: Two details catch people. The stop goes a few cents under the undercut low of 38.31, not exactly on it. And the buy is as price trades through the trigger, never at the close.

reasons: the trigger (D-003), the setup's stop (D-008) and the ALB numbers (D-007) are held; keyed on the settled house rules

wrong.Wait two weeks and recheck: The reclaim is the trigger, and it came on Monday.
wrong.Buy Monday's open, under the low: The open is still under the flush low. We buy the reclaim back above it.

questions.simple: Buy the Monday reclaim. The stock broke under the flush low, then closed back above it, and that is the turn.

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the chart ends on a flush day on heavy volume. Watch it, or pass?

Pass; a slow grind with no burst
Watch it; buy the next green close
Buy the close; the volume marks the low

wrong.Pass; a slow grind with no burst: Look again: three lower closes ending in a 2.41 ATR bar.
wrong.Watch it; buy the next green close: The buy is the reclaim of the flush low within 3 sessions, not a green close.
wrong.Buy the close; the volume marks the low: We never buy the flush close. Nearly half of flush closes are undercut the next day.

questions.simple: Watch it, because it is a fast flush into a real level, and the buy only comes on a later reclaim.

deeper.example: This flush had three lower closes into the round number 100 and the 200-day. It ran 2.41 ATR on 2.25x volume. The next day it undercut the flush low and closed 6% higher, and that reclaim was the buy, not the flush close.

reasons: a chart example from the owner-unreviewed dossier (D-007)

questions.q: Hidden ticker; a flush day: 2.95 ATR, 2.23x volume, the low 12.9% under the 10-day high close. Watch it, or pass?
choices: Pass; only a pullback in a leader
Pass; 2.23x volume is too light
Watch it; 2.95 ATR is a deep flush
Watch it; 12.9% is close enough

questions.why: Pass. The volume and the ATR clear their bars. But the low was only 12.9% under the 10-day high close, and a stock needs 15%. It was a dip to the rising 50-day in a leader: a pullback, not a capitulation.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume and a deep ATR still need the 15% stretch.

wrong.Pass; 2.23x volume is too light: 2.23x clears the 2x volume bar. The stretch is what fails.
wrong.Watch it; 2.95 ATR is a deep flush: The ATR clears 2, but the stretch is short of 15%.
wrong.Watch it; 12.9% is close enough: A rule is a line. The stretch needs 15%, and 12.9% is short of it.

deeper.counter: Big volume and a deep ATR bar look like panic. Here the low was only 12.9% under the 10-day high close, a dip to the rising 50-day in a leader. That is a pullback. A capitulation needs the 15% stretch as well, and no other gate stands in for it.

reasons: a chart near miss from the owner-unreviewed dossier (D-007); the 15% stretch is the dossier's proposal

questions.q: Which flush day reads better on our card?
questions.story: Two stocks flush on 2.3 times their 50-day average volume. For one, that is the biggest volume bar of the whole decline. For the other, an earlier day in the same decline traded more.
choices: The one with no heavier day before
The one with the earlier heavy day
Both read the same; both pass
Neither; it needs 3x to count
questions.answer: The one with no heavier day before
questions.why: The one with no heavier day before it. Both pass the floor of at least 2 times the 50-day average. The card's ideal goes further: the highest volume of the decline or of the year. When an earlier day of the decline traded more, the flush day was not the peak of the selling.
questions.lesson_line: Pass the 2x bar, then look for the biggest bar of the decline.

wrong.The one with the earlier heavy day: An earlier day of the decline traded more, so the flush day was not the peak.
wrong.Neither; it needs 3x to count: The card's floor is at least 2 times the 50-day average. 2.3 times clears it.
wrong.Both read the same; both pass: Both pass the floor of 2 times the 50-day average. The card's ideal is the highest volume of the decline.

questions.simple: The one with no heavier day before it, because the card's best flush day is the heaviest of the decline.

deeper.trap: Passing the 2x floor does not make a day the climax. The card's ideal is the highest volume of the decline or of the year. A flush day beaten by an earlier day meets the floor but misses the ideal.

reasons: the 2x volume is a proposal that may change

questions.q: Our card's best flush day has the highest volume of the decline, or of the year.
questions.why: True. Our card says the flush day ideally has the highest volume of the decline or of the year. That is a mark of the best ones, not the gate. The gate is volume of at least 2 times the 50-day average.
questions.lesson_line: The best flush bar is the biggest bar of the decline.
questions.simple: True, because our card says the best flush day has the most volume of the decline or the year.

reasons: the 2x gate is the dossier's proposal

questions.q: A bounce trade in a stock that averages 400,000 shares a day. Under our 1% rule, what is the most we can own?
questions.why: 4,000 shares. One percent of 400,000 is 4,000. Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. It is a ceiling on the position, whatever the stop would allow.
questions.lesson_line: Size to the stock's volume. One percent of the daily average is the ceiling.
questions.simple: You can own at most 4,000 shares, because that is 1% of the 400,000 shares it trades a day.

questions.q: Our 1% volume rule caps your risk, not how many shares you own.
questions.why: False. It caps the shares: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. Your risk comes from the stop, a separate step.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of average daily volume caps the shares you own.
questions.simple: False, because the 1% rule limits how many shares you own, measured against the stock's daily volume.

questions.q: Do you take the fourth try?
questions.story: You tried the same stock three times this week and were stopped each time. On Friday it reclaims its flush low again.
choices: No; three tries a week is the limit
Yes; a new reclaim is a trigger
Yes, at half size for less risk
No; a stop-out bars a retry
questions.answer: No; three tries a week is the limit
questions.why: No. On one stock we take at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. Each try needs a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop. A fresh reclaim is a new trigger, but the weekly limit still holds. A smaller size does not reset the count.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one name. The fourth waits.

wrong.Yes; a new reclaim is a trigger: A new trigger is needed, but the week's limit still holds: at most 3 tries.
wrong.Yes, at half size for less risk: Half size does not change the count. It is at most 3 tries in a week on one stock.
wrong.No; a stop-out bars a retry: A stop-out does not bar the stock. We buy again on a new trigger, up to 3 tries a week.

questions.simple: No. We take at most three tries a week on one stock, and this would be the fourth.

questions.q: On one stock we allow at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.why: True. A new try needs a new trigger, and the limit is 3 in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: Three a week, six a month, each on a new trigger.

questions.q: A later test of the climax trades below the climax low. What does the Wyckoff school expect?
choices: New lows or prolonged consolidation
A fast bounce back to the 20 EMA
A higher low and a strong rally
A confirmed bottom and a new uptrend
questions.why: New lows or prolonged consolidation. If the test goes lower than the climax, expect either.
questions.lesson_line: A test below the climax low means new lows or a long wait.

wrong.A fast bounce back to the 20 EMA: A test below the climax low is a warning, not a bounce signal.
wrong.A higher low and a strong rally: A higher low needs the test to hold above the climax low. This one went under it.
wrong.A confirmed bottom and a new uptrend: A climax must be successfully tested first. A lower test is not a success.

questions.q: What happens now?
questions.story: You bought the reclaim with the stop a few cents under the low of your entry session. Next morning the stock opens above that low, then trades through your stop.
choices: The stop is the exit; you are out
Wait for a close under the low
Move the stop lower to give room
Hold; the gap rule sets the stop
questions.answer: The stop is the exit; you are out
questions.why: You are out. After the entry, a trade below the low of the entry session is the stop and the exit. It does not wait for a close. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is a gap against the stop, and this stock opened above the low.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit. It does not wait for a close.

wrong.Wait for a close under the low: A close is not the test. The stop is the exit once price trades through it.
wrong.Move the stop lower to give room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Hold; the gap rule sets the stop: It opened above the low, so there was no gap. The gap rule is the one exception, and it does not apply.

questions.simple: You are out. The stop is the exit, and it does not wait for a close.

deeper.trap: Two habits break this rule: waiting for a close under the low, and moving the stop to give it room. Both widen the loss you planned. The only exception is a gap. If the stock opens under the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: the capitulation stop is held under D-008

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: T2108 is the percent of stocks above their ___-day average.
questions.why: 40. T2108 is the percent of stocks above their 40-day average. Our card reads it near or under 15% to 20% as breadth washed out, one backdrop for a market-wide flush.
questions.lesson_line: T2108 counts stocks above their 40-day average. Low readings are washed out.
questions.simple: It is 40, because T2108 is the percent of stocks above their 40-day average.

questions.q: What does breadth say about this market?
questions.story: The Nasdaq is down five days in a row. T2108, a breadth gauge, closes at 17%.
choices: Washed out; it backs a flush
Mild; only 17% of stocks look weak
Too high; it must go under 15%
Beside the point; price decides

questions.lesson_line: Near 15% to 20% on T2108 is washed out.

wrong.Too high; it must go under 15%: The card says near or under 15% to 20%. 17% is in that zone.
wrong.Beside the point; price decides: The card lists washed-out breadth as part of the backdrop for a market-wide flush.
wrong.Mild; only 17% of stocks look weak: T2108 counts stocks above their 40-day average. At 17%, most stocks sit below it.

questions.simple: Washed out. A T2108 reading of 17% sits in the zone the card wants for a market-wide flush.

questions.q: Which flush does our card favor?
questions.story: Two leading stocks flush on heavy volume in different weeks. In one week the index holds above its recent lows. In the other, the index breaks to a new low.
choices: The one with the index holding up
The one with the index breaking down
Both; the index is not part of it
Neither; the index must be stretched too
questions.answer: The one with the index holding up
questions.why: The one with the index holding up. For a single leading stock's flush, the card wants the index holding up or itself stretched, not breaking down. An index making a new low on rising volume while you hold is listed as an invalidation.
questions.lesson_line: Our card wants the index holding up when a leader flushes.

wrong.The one with the index breaking down: The card wants the index holding up or stretched, not breaking down.
wrong.Both; the index is not part of it: The index is part of the read for a single leading stock.
wrong.Neither; the index must be stretched too: The card says holding up or itself stretched. Either will do, so holding up is enough.

questions.simple: The one with the index holding up. For a leader's flush, the card wants the index holding up or stretched, not breaking down.

deeper.counter: Holding up is not the only pass. The card also accepts an index that is itself stretched. What it rules out is an index breaking down. A new index low on rising volume while you hold is an invalidation.

reasons: the leader flush setting is held under D-002 and D-004

questions.q: Which of these is a box in our burst gate?
choices: A gap down on the climax day
A close under the lower band
15% off the 10-day high
Under the 9 and 20 EMA
questions.answer: A gap down on the climax day
questions.why: A gap down on the climax day. It is one of the 5 burst boxes on our card, the same gate as our parabolic long. The others are 3 or more lower closes, two gaps down in a row, growing losses and rising volume. A close under the lower Bollinger band, the 15% stretch and the short averages are separate checks.
questions.lesson_line: The burst gate counts boxes: lower closes, gaps down, growing losses, rising volume.

wrong.A close under the lower band: A band close is supporting evidence only. It is not one of the burst boxes.
wrong.15% off the 10-day high: That is the stretch, its own check. It is not one of the burst boxes.
wrong.Under the 9 and 20 EMA: Falling under the short averages is its own check, not a burst box.

questions.simple: A gap down on the climax day. It is one of the 5 burst boxes, and the other choices are separate checks.

reasons: the box count is held under D-002

questions.story: A stock closes lower four days in a row. Each of the last two losses is bigger than the day before, and volume rose on both days. Only the flush day opens with a gap down.
questions.q: Which burst box does it miss?
choices: Two gaps down in a row
3 or more lower closes
Losses growing day to day
Volume up 2 days running
questions.answer: Two gaps down in a row
questions.why: Two gaps down in a row. The box needs 2 consecutive opening gaps down, and only the flush day gapped. The story ticks the rest: lower closes in a row, growing losses, rising volume and a climax-day gap.
questions.lesson_line: Count the burst boxes one by one. One gap is not two gaps in a row.

wrong.3 or more lower closes: It closed lower four days in a row, so this box is ticked.
wrong.Losses growing day to day: Each of the last two losses was bigger than the day before, so this box is ticked.
wrong.Volume up 2 days running: Volume rose on each of the last two days, so this box is ticked.

questions.simple: Two gaps down in a row. Only the flush day gapped, and the box needs 2 opening gaps down in a row.

reasons: the box count is held under D-002

wrong.No; Orange means only shorts: Mostly cash and shorts is the Red rule. Orange still allows A+ setups.

questions.simple: No. In an Orange market our rulebook takes only A+ setups, and this one grades below that.

reasons: capitulations in Orange and Red are held under D-023
